Yes. Think of your charcoal grill as a two-zone thermostat: direct heat for searing, indirect heat for holding. Light a chimney of lump charcoal, then dump it onto one side of the grate and leave the other side empty. This creates a hot zone and a cool zone. Keep the bottom vents fully open at start-up, then close them halfway once the coals glow. That slows the burn and gives you a steady 250–300 °F indirect side. Add a few fresh coals every 45 minutes to keep the fire alive.

Use a cheap instant-read thermometer clipped to the lid; when the stack cools below 230 °F, toss in a handful of warm briquettes and open the bottom vents a crack. If it creeps above 320 °F, close the vents until the dial drops. This manual fine-tuning beats fancy thermocouples for most backyard cooks.

For longer sessions, build a “snake” of charcoal: arrange half a brick of briquettes in a curved line along one edge, light the tail, and let the coals burn toward you. The snake keeps the indirect zone stable for three to four hours without adding fuel.
